The proposed radar-absorbing material (RAM) design showed more than -10 dB reflection loss from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies.
Three different rivet configurations were studied: RAS C1 (rivet at the center of unit cell), RAS C2 (rivet between two unit cells), and RAS C3 (rivet at the center of four unit cells).
The study considered three cases with varying the percentage of rivet heads area to RAS surface area: 9.8%, 4.4%, and 2.5%.

Rivet surface area of 9.8% led to significant degradation in reflection coefficient across the frequencies at normal incidence, while rivet surface area of 4.4% and 2.5% showed maximum degradation of 5 dB and 3 dB, respectively.
The flat panel RAS sample showed mono-static RCS reduction of 0 dB and 0 dB at normal incidence for horizontal (HH) and vertical (VV) polarizations, respectively.
The mono-static RCS of the RAS air intake duct showed improvement with an increase in duct length, with the RAS C1 configuration showing the worst performance.

The median RCS of the RAS air intake duct showed a reduction of approximately 10 dB from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies compared to the PEC air intake duct when installed on the open-source aircraft CAD model.
The impact of rivets was found to be negligible on the RCS performance of the RAS air intake duct when installed on the open-source aircraft CAD model.

The study suggests that further research on different shapes, sizes, and patterns of rivets installed on air intake ducts, as well as the impact of rivets on low-observable aircraft, are open research areas.
The high-frequency electromagnetic simulations using the shooting and bouncing rays method were employed for the analysis of the air intake duct cavities.
The study considered air intake ducts of different lengths (1 m, 4 m, etc.) to investigate the impact of duct length on the RCS performance.
The open-source aircraft CAD model was used to evaluate the performance of the RAS air intake with and without rivets, and the results were compared with the aircraft having a non-RAS air intake.
The RAS air intake showed a mono-static RCS reduction of around 10 dB from ϕ=180 degree (nose of the aircraft) to ϕ=240 degree when installed on the open-source aircraft CAD model.
The study found that the RAS air intake showed better RCS performance compared to the PEC air intake duct when installed on the open-source aircraft CAD model.
The impact of rivets on the RCS performance was found to be negligible for the open-source aircraft CAD model, but the authors suggest that the impact may be significant for a low-RCS aircraft model.
